title: Did Marie Antoinette Really Say "Let Them Eat Cake"? The Scene Predates Her by 15 Years
description:
"If there's no bread, let them eat cake." It's almost always pinned on Marie Antoinette. Only what's on record: after the 1775 Flour War, the queen wrote her mother twice that bread was dear and the people suffered greatly. The earliest text we can find naming her: Karr's Les Guêpes, November 1841, calling it hearsay, true or false; in 1843 he wrote that this more or less proved she never said it. Earlier, Book Six of Rousseau's Confessions (published 1782) gives it to just "a great princess"; the scene where Rousseau recalls it is Lyon, around 1740, 15 years before the queen was born.

Rousseau wrote brioche (bread with butter and eggs); English versions of 1783 and 1903 say pastry. Part One dates to the late 1760s; the year of Book Six is uncertain, hence "ten or so" and "under 13". Rousseau admitted Part One, written from memory, had many errors; that he made it up is only scholars' suspicion. Karr gives the 1760 book no title, and we haven't found it; researchers say Revolution-era pamphlets lack the line, and Karr's "back then" gives no year. Madame Victoire's line is secondhand, from the Countess de Boigne's memoir. Whether Marie Antoinette said anything at other times, the record can't say; but Rousseau's princess cannot be her. Wikipedia sources below are secondhand. "I think" and "we think" lines are our opinion.

AI-generated illustrations: historical figures are unnamed cartoons, not likenesses; no modern researchers.

mb101.text: You've surely heard it: no bread? Then let them eat cake. A line a queen still carries today.

mb103.text: Yet the earliest text we can find that pins it on her came 48 years after she died.

mb104.text: In 1740, in Lyon, France, a young tutor secretly drank his master's white wine.

mb105.text: He always had to eat with his wine.

mb106.text: But he dared not enter a bakery; he passed 30 pastry shops without going in.

mb107.text: He wore a sword. Why didn't he dare buy a piece of bread?

mb108.text: But that's not the strangest part. In 1775, the queen wrote her mother about bread.

mb109.text: In 1782, a book was printed in Geneva. Its author was already dead.

mb110.text: This file tracks the line back 100 years, to the door of a pastry shop.

mb111.text: Did Marie Antoinette really say "Let them eat cake"?

mb201.text: In the legend, the French people were short of bread when she said it. Did such days really exist?

mb202.text: Yes, that very spring: she'd been queen for less than a year, and bread prices rose.

mb203.text: How vital was bread? Biographers estimate ordinary people then spent half their income on it.

mb204.text: Imagine your biggest monthly bill suddenly rose: would you take to the streets?

mb205.text: That's why biographers call bread the top concern of the entire nation.

mb206.text: The spark: the September before, the state freed the grain trade.

mb207.text: Then from April to May, riots broke out in many places in the north, east and west;

mb208.text: In early May, crowds reached the gates of Versailles.

mb209.text: Next day, Paris bakeries were looted too.

mb210.text: Later, people called it the Flour War.

mb211.text: Those who study her say the unrest hurt her name with the people.

mb212.text: Later anti-royal pamphlets even dubbed her "Madame Deficit," saying she alone drained France's money.

mb213.text: I think that's why this line sticks to her: foreign-born, a big spender, and the queen.

mb214.text: So did she herself know how expensive bread was?

mb301.text: She knew, and she wrote it down. That June 11, the king was crowned;

mb302.text: Eleven days later, the letter to her mother from the start is dated June 22.

mb303.text: Her mother was Austria's empress, Maria Theresa; these letters were only published together in 1866.

mb304.text: She wrote: two months after the riots, people still welcome us so warmly; sadly, bread is still dear.

mb305.text: "Seeing people who suffer yet treat us so well, we owe it all the more to work for their happiness."

mb306.text: She added that the king seemed to grasp it deeply, too.

mb307.text: Did she write about bread only once?

mb308.text: No. Three weeks later she wrote again: people suffered a lot because bread was so dear.

mb309.text: "Luckily wheat's fine; after harvest bread will surely cost less."

mb310.text: Honestly, they surprised me a bit on first read.

mb315.text: A queen of 19 wrote them, and she didn't sound like she'd say "eat cake."

mb311.text: So do these two letters prove she never said it?

mb312.text: No. The letters show her attitude, not what she said.

mb313.text: Your letter to Mom only shows your thoughts that day.

mb314.text: So the text that pinned it on her, 48 years after her death: who wrote it?

mb401.text: It was written by a man named Karr, in November 1841.

mb402.text: In his journal Les Guêpes, he wrote: people say Marie Antoinette once made a remark, true or not—

mb404.text: Brioche is a bread made with butter and eggs, a luxury food back then, but not cake.

mb405.text: So where did the "cake" come from?

mb406.text: By then, 48 years had passed since her death in 1793, just as I said at the start.

mb407.text: Note his wording: people say, true or not. Karr was passing it on, not inventing it.

mb409.text: Researchers say the line isn't in French Revolution-era pamphlets.

mb410.text: That's odd: by this account, the years that hated her most are where it's missing.

mb411.text: If you wrote pamphlets slamming her back then, wouldn't you use a line this good?

mb412.text: Two years later, Karr wrote another article. What did he say?

mb501.text: It was 1843. He recalled that back then, someone spread a rumor

mb502.text: that on hearing "the people" had no bread, she said it; but he never said which year "back then" was.

mb503.text: He added that a few days before, he'd chanced on a book dated 1760,

mb504.text: which attributed the same line to a duchess of Tuscany.

mb505.text: Karr wrote: this more or less proves the line wasn't Marie Antoinette's, but was found and used against her.

mb506.text: See, now it gets interesting: the earliest person we can find who pinned it on her said, two years later, it probably wasn't her.

mb508.text: Karr gave no title; we didn't find it.

mb509.text: But nearly 60 years before Karr, a book you can still open today put this line in black and white.

mb601.text: It's the Geneva book from the start: Rousseau's Confessions.

mb602.text: When Part One came out, Rousseau had been dead four years.

mb603.text: Book Six says: a great princess, told the peasants had no bread,

mb604.text: replied: then let them eat brioche.

mb605.text: A Lausanne edition that same year has it too.

mb606.text: Note his verb: "I recalled." He wasn't recording fresh news; he was digging up an old memory.

mb607.text: So who was this great princess?

mb608.text: Rousseau doesn't say: no name, no country, no year.

mb609.text: Remember Karr's "the people"? In Rousseau, they were only peasants.

mb610.text: See, in 60 years on the road, the line even changed who it was about.

mb611.text: As for the cake, it came from translation: the first English version, in 1783, said "pastry";

mb612.text: The 1903 English version still said "pastry" too.

mb613.text: Oddly, the 1783 version, in the same passage, also calls the brioche "a bit of cake";

mb614.text: Only later did "cake" become its usual translation.

mb615.text: So when was Book Six written?

mb701.text: The late 1760s. First in rural England, then in a castle, Rousseau wrote Part One.

mb702.text: The early books were written in England from March 1766 to the next May;

mb712.text: Whether Book Six was also finished there, no one can say.

mb703.text: What's certain: in Book Six he says that while writing, he was frail and nearly 60.

mb704.text: Think about it: an old man writing about his own twenties.

mb705.text: And where was Marie Antoinette then?

mb706.text: Born in Vienna in 1755, she was still there, a little girl of ten or so.

mb707.text: In April 1770 she was married by proxy in Vienna; only in May did she reach Versailles, aged 14.

mb708.text: So when Rousseau wrote of that princess, Marie Antoinette was under 13 and had never been to France.

mb709.text: When the book came out, she was 26 and had been queen for 8 years.

mb710.text: Neat, isn't it? When the book came out, readers had a queen right there.

mb711.text: But when was it that Rousseau remembered this line?

mb801.text: Remember the young tutor at the start, who didn't dare buy bread? He was Rousseau.

mb802.text: He came to Lyon in May 1740, lived with the provost, taught two pupils, and left a year later.

mb803.text: He was sneaking his master's little Jura white wine; by his own account, it was very good.

mb804.text: He wrote: a respectable gentleman wearing a sword, walking into a bakery to buy bread? How could he?

mb805.text: You've likely felt it: too dressed up to walk into a small shop.

mb806.text: He went out alone just for that bread, sometimes crossing the whole town.

mb807.text: And to go in, there had to be only one person inside, with a face he found very pleasing.

mb808.text: Finally, recalling the princess's words as a last resort, he bought brioche.

mb809.text: He wasn't mocking her; he used her line to save face.

mb811.text: That opening scene was around 1740, 15 years before Marie Antoinette was even born.

mb812.text: Sure, Rousseau wrote from memory 20-plus years on; he admitted Part One must have many errors.

mb813.text: Some scholars even suspect he made the story up.

mb814.text: All that's certain: when writing the book, he already knew this tale.

mb815.text: Honestly, that a tale of stolen wine and bread became charges against a queen amazes me every time.

mb816.text: So does any record actually name who said it?

mb901.text: One does. A countess's memoir names her: Louis XV's daughter, Madame Victoire.

mb902.text: The countess called her not very bright, but extremely kind.

mb903.text: She wrote that during a food shortage,

mb904.text: Madame Victoire, hearing the poor had no bread, said in tears:

mb905.text: "My God, if only they could settle for meat pie crust!"

mb906.text: How does it differ from your version?

mb907.text: The crust is the pastry shell around a meat pie.

mb908.text: Here, the speaker isn't callous but kind.

mb910.text: The countess who wrote the memoir was born only in 1781; she heard this secondhand.

mb911.text: She began writing in 1835, and the memoir was only published in 1907.

mb912.text: We think the line kept seeking an owner because people needed a princess unaware of bread prices.

mb913.text: So, the opening question: did Marie Antoinette really say it?

mb914.text: Whether she ever said anything offhand in her life, records can't tell us.

mb915.text: But the line in that book can't be about her.

mb917.text: Where'd you first hear it, and from whom? Tell me below.

mb918.text: This channel sticks to the record. To open files together, subscribe.
